slides.label: Introduction to the Global Gauss-Bonnet Theorem
slides.notes: Open by naming the surprise of the chapter: a quantity obtained by integrating local Gaussian curvature over a closed surface returns a purely topological number. The lecture should frame pages 165 to 174 as a change in scale, from local bending measurements to a global invariant that ignores the particular embedding.

slides.label: From Local Curvature to a Global Ledger
slides.notes: Use this slide to slow down the bookkeeping. Gaussian curvature is still the pointwise product of principal curvatures, but the global theorem asks for the signed area under that function over the whole surface. The crucial shift is that positive and negative patches are allowed to cancel before topology enters.

slides.label: The Theorem in One Line
slides.notes: State the theorem cleanly, then unpack each term. The left side is analytic and metric: integrate Gaussian curvature against the area element. The right side is combinatorial and topological: Euler characteristic. Emphasize that the equality is for closed oriented surfaces here, so boundary terms are absent.

slides.label: Euler Characteristic as Surface Memory
slides.notes: Read the local figure as an invariant catalog rather than as a taxonomy poster. The sphere, torus, and higher genus examples have different Euler characteristics, and Gauss-Bonnet turns those integers into prescribed total curvature budgets. The surface may be stretched or redrawn, but the ledger total remains pinned.

slides.label: Calibrating on the Sphere
slides.notes: Use the spherical map figure to make the normalization feel inevitable. On the unit sphere, Gaussian curvature is one everywhere, so total curvature is just spherical area, four pi. That matches two pi times Euler characteristic two, giving a first calibration before more subtle cancellation examples.

slides.label: Torus: Cancellation Without Flatness
slides.notes: This slide prevents a common misconception. The torus has total curvature zero, but that does not mean it is flat as an embedded surface. Positive curvature on the outside and negative curvature on the inside cancel in the integral, which is exactly what Euler characteristic zero predicts.

slides.label: Handles Change the Curvature Budget
slides.notes: The pancake-and-hole figure makes the sign bookkeeping tactile. Every added handle lowers Euler characteristic by two, so the total curvature decreases by four pi. Speak of handles as changing the accounting rule, not as tiny local defects, because the theorem constrains the whole closed surface.

slides.label: Gauss Map Degree
slides.notes: Introduce the Gauss map as the bridge between geometry and topology. A normal direction at each point of the surface lands on the unit sphere. Counting signed covering of the sphere gives a degree, and the curvature integral measures that signed covering area. This is the conceptual route into later proofs.

slides.label: What the Theorem Lets Us Predict
slides.notes: Close by turning the theorem into a diagnostic. Given the topology, the total curvature is already determined, even before choosing a specific shape. Given a proposed curvature distribution, the theorem tests whether it can belong to a closed surface of that genus. Preview that the next chapter explains why this accounting works.
